description: Labeled RAG eval set for DS/ML interview concept corpus. Gold answers are grounded in corpus docs.

items.question: What is the bias-variance tradeoff?
items.gold_answer: Bias measures systematic error from overly simple models (underfitting); variance measures sensitivity to training set changes (overfitting). Expected error decomposes into bias squared plus variance plus noise. Regularization and model complexity control the tradeoff.

items.question: How does L1 regularization differ from L2?
items.gold_answer: L2 (Ridge) shrinks weights toward zero without eliminating them and helps with multicollinearity. L1 (Lasso) encourages sparsity so many coefficients become exactly zero, enabling feature selection. Elastic Net combines both.

items.question: What is k-fold cross-validation and when use stratified folds?
items.gold_answer: K-fold CV splits data into K parts, training on K-1 and validating on one fold, rotating through all folds. Stratified K-fold preserves class proportions and is preferred for imbalanced classification.

items.question: Define precision, recall, and F1 score.
items.gold_answer: Precision is TP/(TP+FP); recall is TP/(TP+FN). F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Accuracy can mislead on imbalanced data, so choose metrics based on the cost of false positives versus false negatives.

items.question: What does ROC AUC measure?
items.gold_answer: ROC AUC summarizes ranking quality as the probability a random positive ranks above a random negative. It is threshold-independent. PR-AUC is often more informative when positives are rare.

items.question: Explain how retrieval-augmented generation works.
items.gold_answer: RAG retrieves relevant documents and conditions a generator on that context to reduce hallucination and update knowledge without retraining. The pipeline chunks, embeds, indexes, retrieves top-k, then generates an answer from context.

items.question: What is BM25 and why combine it with dense retrieval?
items.gold_answer: BM25 is a probabilistic lexical ranker using term frequency saturation, length normalization, and IDF. It is strong on exact keywords but weak on synonyms. Hybrid BM25 plus dense embeddings improves robustness via fusion such as RRF.

items.question: Why is document chunking important in RAG systems?
items.gold_answer: Chunking splits long documents into passages that fit embedding and context windows while preserving coherence. Too-small chunks lose context; too-large chunks dilute relevance. Metadata like doc_id and section support citation.

items.question: How do you handle imbalanced classification datasets?
items.gold_answer: Prefer precision, recall, F1, or PR-AUC over accuracy. Techniques include class weights, SMOTE oversampling, undersampling, and threshold tuning. Collecting more minority examples and better features often beats resampling alone.

items.question: What is the difference between bagging and boosting?
items.gold_answer: Bagging averages diverse models on bootstrap samples to reduce variance (e.g., Random Forest). Boosting sequentially fits models to residuals to reduce bias (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM). Stacking uses a meta-learner on base predictions.

items.question: How does self-attention work in transformers?
items.gold_answer: Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(QK transpose over sqrt(d)) times V. Multi-head attention runs several projections in parallel. Transformers enable parallel sequence processing and capture long-range dependencies.

items.question: What metrics are used to evaluate RAG systems?
items.gold_answer: RAG evaluation covers context relevance or precision, faithfulness of the answer to retrieved context, and answer relevance to the question. Also report retrieval recall@k. Offline labeled sets enable regression testing without paid APIs.

items.question: What is data leakage in machine learning?
items.gold_answer: Leakage uses information unavailable at prediction time, inflating offline metrics. Examples include scaling before the split, target-derived features, and future timestamps. Fit transformers inside CV folds and use time-aware splits.

items.question: Explain cosine similarity for text retrieval.
items.gold_answer: Cosine similarity is the cosine of the angle between vectors, focusing on orientation rather than magnitude. It is useful when document length varies. With L2-normalized embeddings, cosine equals the dot product.

items.question: What is probability calibration?
items.gold_answer: A classifier is calibrated if predicted probabilities match empirical frequencies. Reliability diagrams, Brier score, and ECE measure miscalibration. Platt scaling, isotonic regression, and temperature scaling recalibrate scores.

items.question: How does A/B testing estimate causal lift?
items.gold_answer: A/B tests randomly assign users to variants and compare metrics. Power analysis sets sample size from baseline, MDE, alpha, and power. Avoid naive peeking; use guardrail metrics and methods like CUPED to reduce variance.

items.question: What is a feature store and why use one?
items.gold_answer: A feature store centralizes feature definitions and online/offline serving with point-in-time correctness. It reduces training-serving skew by reusing the same transforms and supports versioning and lineage.

items.question: Why prefer PR-AUC when positives are rare?
items.gold_answer: When positives are rare, ROC AUC can look optimistic because false positive rate stays low even with many false positives. Precision-recall AUC focuses on performance among predicted positives and is more informative for rare events.

items.question: What causes vanishing gradients and how to mitigate them?
items.gold_answer: Vanishing gradients occur when gradients shrink through deep stacks of saturating activations like sigmoid. Mitigations include ReLU, residual connections, careful initialization, and batch normalization.

items.question: How does reciprocal rank fusion help hybrid retrieval?
items.gold_answer: RRF merges ranked lists from different retrievers such as BM25 and dense embeddings without needing calibrated scores. It is commonly used after retrieving candidates and before or instead of cross-encoder reranking.
